idiom_name: let constant stored properties and private(set)
implementation_notes: Swift expresses the pattern directly: a stored property declared with `let` is a constant that can be assigned during initialization and never afterwards - a subclass cannot modify an inherited `let` at all - and `private(set)` keeps a `var` publicly readable while restricting writes to the declaring scope, which is exactly the read/write asymmetry the pattern asks for. Value types strengthen it further: because a `struct` is copied, handing a struct value to another component gives it a snapshot that cannot be mutated back into the original, so a read-only holder should hold value types. Use `let` for state fixed at construction and `private(set)` for state the type legitimately updates internally (counters, caches), and keep the classic two-object form only when several fields must be validated as one unit.
pitfalls: `let` freezes the binding, not the referenced object: a `let` array can still be appended to if it is a `var`-typed reference, and a `let` class instance can still be mutated through its methods.
`private(set)` restricts writes to the enclosing declaration and same-file extensions, whereas `fileprivate(set)` is wider than it reads and `internal(set)` is no protection at all within the module.
Reference types break the snapshot guarantee: two references to the same class instance share its state, so a read-only holder must hold value types or implement copy-on-write.
